articles.text: It is reported that 200 Indians have left their reserve at Battle river and gone to join Big Bear.
articles.summary: Report that 200 Indians left the Battle River reserve to join Big Bear (Canadian North-West rebellion).

articles.text:
A soap mine has been discovered out on Beaver creek, about ten miles from here. It is of a whitish color, and having been tested by all the settlers, is is pronounced a genuine substitute for the manufactured article.—[Sundance Gazette.

If this is a bonafide discovery and not soft soap, we shall hope to see the Gazette come out next week with a clean sheet.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Sundance Gazette about a 'soap mine' on Beaver Creek, with a joking comment by the Cow Boy.

articles.text: There never was a time in the history of our country when there has been such a demand for horses, in the east as well as the west, as at present. In order to keep up the supply, especially for the eastern markets, the east and west will have to combine. The east to supply the stallions best adapted to the greatest demand, while the west can furnish mares sufficiently good, that when bred to a thoroughbred stallion, will produce horses, surpassed by none for beauty, size and endurance.
articles.summary: On the strong demand for horses and breeding western mares to eastern thoroughbred stallions.

articles.text: A correspondent of the Live Stock Journal, England, who has been looking up the history of the polled breeds of cattle, finds that hornless cattle have been known for many centuries. A Greek coin of Mytilene, of the fifth century, B. C. which he has seen, has on the obverse, the heads of two hornless cattle. As far back as 2700 B. C., the Egyptians had hornless cattle depicted on their monuments, which would give the breed a history more than 4,500 years old. Twenty-three centuries ago there were known to be polled breeds of cattle in Siberia, and it is believed now, that they were kept in that cold climate in preference to the horned breeds, because they could endure the cold far better than cattle with horns. Hippocrates makes mention of "chariots drawn by oxen which had no horns," and says that the "cold prevents them from having any." It is very evident that the polled cattle are in no sense of modern origin, but that they existed beyond the date of any written history.
articles.summary: On the ancient history of polled (hornless) cattle, after the English Live Stock Journal.

articles.text: The north, west and northwest has long been an outlet for Texas cattle, and trail drivers in the early days all started their herds as early in the season as grass would permit and foremen tried to see who could bring his herd through in the best condition. Those were days when cattle were driven by the purchaser. At present cattle are nearly all driven by contractors and not much regard is paid to the time of starting and herds are rushed through in far too short a time, as a late movement of stock is seldom profitable to the parties finally ranching the cattle, unless a very mild winter follows the drive, and for several years the drive has been getting later and later. This is a very serious error that many ranchmen make, and it is only dear-bought experience that impresses upon the minds of cattle should be on the range not later than the first of August, as it takes stock some time to locate on a new range. They should be well rested and located before winter. Now in order to do this purchaser should make it his interest to see that his cattle start early enough to get here in the right season and specify the time for passing certain points. We think losses would be much less on southern cattle were they properly handled.
articles.summary: Argues that Texas trail herds should reach northern ranges by August 1 and that late, contractor-driven drives cause losses.

articles.headline: Taxes.
articles.text: The following is in reply to an inquiry sent Sec'y. Teller, a few days ago in regard to the taxes that have been levied on Billings county by Morton and Stark counties. "Chapter 81 of 1883 authorizes commissioners of organized counties to grant liquor licenses in unorganized counties which are attached to them for judicial purposes, though nothing is said as to which organized county shall grant such license. There has been no change in this law so far as I know. An act was passed by the last legislature, providing for the assessment of taxes in unorganized counties." From the above, it would seem that the assessments that have been made are both legal, and now it only remains to be decided whether the taxes we are to pay, together with the railroad tax, would be sufficient to run an organized county of our own, or whether it is better to pay for the support of other counties. The railroad tax of this county amounts to about $4,000. The saloon tax at the present time amounts to $1,400. The personal property tax levied by Stark county will possibly amount to $2,500, making a total of $7,900. On two sides of us are unorganized counties from which we would be entitled to collect taxes. The stockmen of this county should look into this matter thoroughly and find out if they are not "buttering some body else's bread," as they are the ones most interested. Will it be better for them to control the amount of their own taxes or let some other county with a large debt to pay, do it for them. We have no school, in a county twenty-five miles wide by eighty miles long. We would be glad to have some one present the other side of the question, as we have only touched one side of it. The "balance of power" in this county will always, it is to be hoped, be in the hands of the stockmen as it is now. The motive in qringing this matter to their attention is with the hope they will give the matter a careful investigation and if any steps are necessary for their own protection, take them in time.
articles.summary: Reply from Secretary Teller on Morton and Stark county taxes levied on unorganized Billings County, with the Cow Boy urging stockmen to consider organizing the county.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. Annoncement.
articles.text:
Cattle-men of the Little Missouri river are advised that the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company, will give them during June for the beef and dry cows that they wish to sell, Chicago prices less seventy cents per hundred to cover freight and shrinkage. The cattle to be delivered in the evening at the Sully Creek corrals and weighed in the morning.

Marquis de Mores, President.
articles.summary: Notice signed by the Marquis de Morès that the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company will buy beef and dry cows in June at Chicago prices less 70 cents per hundred, delivered at the Sully Creek corrals.

articles.text: The spring round-up of the Smoky Hill pool has been completed and the total loss of cattle, in naerly twenty thousand head, has proven to be less than five per cent.—[Kansas Cow Boy.
articles.summary: Smoky Hill pool spring round-up shows losses under five percent (Kansas Cow Boy).

articles.text: Twenty-six car loads of cattle (two-year olds) belonging to Evans, Hunter & Co., passed through Dodge, last Monday night on their way from Comanche county, enroute for the company's range in Montana.—[Kansas Cow Boy.
articles.summary: Evans, Hunter & Co. cattle shipped through Dodge City for Montana (Kansas Cow Boy).

articles.text: Eleven cars cattle belonging to Parker & Co., passed Medora last Monday, en route to Miles City. The cattle were all graded stock from Kentucky, seven cars of which were from Lexington, and amongst the lot were two cars of fine Short-Horn bulls.
articles.summary: Eleven cars of Kentucky graded cattle for Parker & Co. passed Medora Monday bound for Miles City.

articles.text: The blackleg has appeared in the eastern portion of Ford county. Five yearlings and twos have died on the ranch of the Bergen Brothers. The cattle were purhased in the spring of Mr. Schaeffor, and were in bad condition at the time of the purchase. They fattened rapidly on the spring grass, which is what's the matter.—[Kansas Cow Boy.
articles.summary: Blackleg in Ford County, Kansas (Kansas Cow Boy).

articles.text: Texas cattlemen are still followed by an adverse fate. Just as they had made arrangements for opening a market in Cuba for a very considerable number of beef steers the government of that country sees an opportunity to gather in a few needed sheckels and lays on a heavy import duty, the new rule to be put in effect on and after July 1st, 1885.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Cuba imposes an import duty on Texas beef steers from July 1, 1885 (N. W. Live Stock Journal).

articles.text: To illustrate the horse business in this country: Sheriff Ryan, who has a band of good ones, tells us that four years ago he bought a mare for $125. She has produced four colts, one of which he sold for $200; was offered $250 for another, and has the yearling and suckling, worth $250, and aside from the interest on the amount paid for the mare, has not cost $20 to raise the whole outfit.—[Sundance Gazette.
articles.summary: Sheriff Ryan's profitable mare, as an illustration of the horse business (Sundance Gazette).

articles.text: Two Frenchmen have landed in New York with a fortune invested in fifty-seven head of horses. They intend starting a horse ranch in Montana having already purchased the land. Montana is getting to be a great ranching country, and is laying claim to equality in horse and cattle raising importance. There is no denying that they have captured some heavy investments in the way of ranching.—[Globe L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Two Frenchmen bring 57 horses to start a Montana horse ranch (Globe Live Stock Journal).

articles.text: Latest returns to the statistician at Washington show an increase in the number of horses and mules in nearly every state in the union. The average increase in horses is about four per cent. Compared with last year the unmber is 11,564,572 head, against 11,169,683 head, an increase of 394,889. Values have decreased from $74.64 to $73.70 per head, a difference of 94 cents. The shrinkage in price is much less on horses than on any other class of live stock, being between one and two per cent.—[Stockgrowers' Journal.
articles.summary: National statistics on increased horse numbers and slightly lower values (Stockgrowers' Journal).

articles.text: The largest exchange of horse flesh that ever took place in Montana was made in Miles City a few days since. Wm. Rowe, of Ft. Benton, gave J. H. Truman for his Shire horse Importer and one grade horse, twenty-nine head of good native Montana horses. Mr. Truman is fascinated with the stock ranges of Montana. For the purpose of introducing good horses into Montana, he is willing to trade, as in the above case, English Shire horses or Polled Angus bulls, for native Montana mares, neat cattle or sheep. This will enable those who have not the ready cash to procure the best blooded animals brought to Montana.—[Ex.
articles.summary: J. H. Truman trades a Shire stallion for 29 native horses at Miles City (exchange).

articles.headline: THE LOST CABIN GOLD MINES. By J. S. WARN.
articles.text:
In the mean time, Hulbert packed his knapsack, buried what gold dust he could not carry conveniently and fled for his life. He knew a trail east to the top of the mountains and by day light the next morning he was far away from the old camp. He could see to the east an open country and to the west of him a range of mountains covered with snow, which he thought at that time to be another spur of the Big Horn mountains. In this however he was mistaken, as he was without doubt, now standing on the Little Wolf mountains. He struck an easterly course and travelled nights, the snow capped mountains remaining in view a long time and finally on the eighteenth day struck the North Platte river [90?] miles above Fort Laramie at Reshaw's bridge, where he found the old trail that he went over in 1849 to California, and also found Reshaw and his family, the first white people he had seen except his two comrades, for many months. Here he heard of the great discovery of gold in the Alder gulch in Montana, and also of the big stampede from the east, coming up the Platte. He rested for a few days bought a horse and saddle and started down the Platte to meet the stampede.

I was among the first who arrived at Ft. Laramie. We had about a dozen wagon loads of pilgrims in our outfit and were waiting for more to come, as the Indians were very hostile and we did not dare to start out without a large crowd. Captain Hulbert came into our camp from the west and told us his story as it has been related in the foregoing account, and showed us the gold which he had. As might be expected it created a great stir in camp and everyone was crazy to start at once for the mines. Accordingly arrangements were made with him to pilot us, as there was no doubt in the mind of any one that his account was true. He was to take us there within twenty days. We waited until we had 140 wagons in the train and 550 men women and children.

The Indians learned that we were going through their country east of the Big Horn mountains and old chief Spotted Tail went to the commander at Ft. Laramie and made a protest. We were ordered not to go and the old chief made a speech, saying that he would fight us every step of the way. Hulbert told him in reply that there were not Indians or soldiers enough on the plains to stop us, and that we were going anyway. We started out and followed the old California trail until we arrived at Reshaw's bridge on the Platte, where we went into camp. It was here that I met Mr. Bozeman for the first time. He had come from Virginia City, Mont., on horse-back to pilot a train of Pilgrims on a short cut to the mines in Alder gulch and was now on his return. It was arranged that Bozeman should remain here and pick up another train of emigrants and follow us as soon as possible. We started on and went slowly, as we had a large train, and had to make roads and bridge streams to get the wagons across. We moved about fifteen miles a day. Captain Hulbert was with me a great deal of the time so that I had ample opportunity to question and talk with him, and had a good idea of where his mines were. He was looked-up to and respected, by the whole party and his word was law in everything. We finally arrived at the foot hills of the Big Horn mountains.

(Continued.)
articles.summary: Installment of J. S. Warn's reminiscence of Captain Hulbert's 'Lost Cabin' gold story and the 1860s emigrant train he guided toward the Big Horn mountains.

articles.text: Mirrors at drug store.
articles.summary: Drug store notice: mirrors.

articles.text: Go to the drug store for paints, oils and varnishes.
articles.summary: Drug store notice: paints, oils and varnishes.

articles.text: Howard Eaton received three car loads of fine bulls last week.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton received three carloads of bulls.

articles.text: Editor BAD LANDS COW BOY and wife are expected home this evening.
articles.summary: Packard and his wife expected home this evening.

articles.text: Col. McClellan will be the first census enumerator for Billings county.
articles.summary: Col. McClellan named first census enumerator for Billings County.

articles.text: Stock inspector W. D. Smith was in Medora inspecting the Hash Knife herd, last Monday.
articles.summary: Stock inspector W. D. Smith inspected the Hash Knife herd at Medora Monday.

articles.text: The firm of Warn & Brown has dissolved partnership. Mr. Brown has returned to his home in Missouri.
articles.summary: Warn & Brown dissolved partnership; Brown returned to Missouri.

articles.text: Col. J. N. Simpson left yesterday morning for his home in Dallas, Texas. He expects to return by the 1st., of July.
articles.summary: Col. J. N. Simpson left for Dallas, to return by July 1.

articles.text: T. D. Jones of Yonkers N. Y. made his Medora friends a visit last week and departed for Meyers, Mont. on last Tuesday.
articles.summary: T. D. Jones of Yonkers visited Medora and left Tuesday for Myers, Montana.

articles.text: Prices at the popular one price clothing store, will be reduced ten per cent for the next thirty days. Give them a call.
articles.summary: Ten percent price cut at the one-price clothing store for thirty days.

articles.text: The boys of the round-up have been having a good time this week as work has been suspended, until the river goes down.
articles.summary: Round-up work suspended this week until the river falls.

articles.text: Dr. H. W. Coe, who represents this district in the Terrstorial legislature is in town in the interests of the census bureau.
articles.summary: Territorial legislator Dr. H. W. Coe in Medora on census business.

articles.text: Some of our young people should remember that the night air is unhealthy and when they go out driving in the park, come home before half past ten.
articles.summary: Teasing advice to young people driving in the park at night.

articles.text: The smokestack at the slaughter-house was completed yesterdry and now the draft is so great it is almost dangerous for a stranger to pass through the boiler room.
articles.summary: Smokestack at the Medora slaughter-house completed.

articles.text: Carpenters have been busy the last few days putting up a building for E. G. Paddock, which will be occupied by T. W. Gordon the enterprising clothing merchant of Medora.
articles.summary: Building going up for E. G. Paddock, to be occupied by clothier T. W. Gordon.

articles.text: The Elk saloon has become the favorite resort in Little Missouri. Go there once and you will need no second urging, as the proprietors keep the best wines, liquors and cigars to be had.
articles.summary: Puff for the Elk saloon in Little Missouri.

articles.text: Medora is becoming quite a resort for tourists and pleasure seekers. Hardly a train passes that does not leave some visitors in tee city, who are generally well pleased with the bad lands.
articles.summary: Medora drawing tourists from nearly every train.

articles.text: There is some talk of a horse race at Medora on the 4th of July. There are quite a number of fast horses on the river that will make a good race. Will some one start a purse and see what can be done.
articles.summary: Talk of a Fourth of July horse race at Medora.

articles.text: We are reliably informed that Fred M. Willard has been appointed stock inspector at this place, by the Montana stock association. Mr. Willard will probably arrive here some day this week to enter upon his duties.
articles.summary: Fred M. Willard appointed Montana stock association inspector at Medora.

articles.text: J. A. Ferris has set men to work digging a cellar twenty-five be sixty feet on his lots on main street, where he intends to erect a store building twenty-five by seventy-five feet, which he intends to occupy as soon as completed.
articles.summary: J. A. Ferris begins a cellar for a 25-by-75-foot store building on Main Street.

articles.text: Jim. Asborne of Glendive Montana was arrested in Jamestown Dak. last week. He had eighty head of horses in his possession to which he could not prove his right of ownership. Jim's reputation for rustling has not been of the best for some time past.
articles.summary: Jim Asborne of Glendive arrested at Jamestown with eighty horses he could not prove were his.

articles.text: A serious accident occurred at the E6 ranch that proved fatal to one of the boys in the employ of that outfit. Just before starting on the round-up one of the boys whose name we failed to learn, received a severe kick on the head, which caused his death not long after.
articles.summary: A cowboy at the E6 ranch died after a kick to the head before the round-up.

articles.text: The stockmens ball last evening at the rink was a grand success. Everybody was there and nothing occurred to mar the enjoyment. The music was good and very much of the pleasure of the evening was due to the efficient services of the floor manager Mr. Frank Smith.
articles.summary: Stockmen's ball at the rink a success; Frank Smith floor manager.

articles.text: C. E. Marvin president of the crescent creamery, Rochester Minn., made us a call this week. He reports business as being very good in his line, having sold 100,000 pounds of butter and cheese on this trip. Their annual sales amount to 1,000,000 pounds of butter and 500,000 pounds of cheese.
articles.summary: C. E. Marvin of the Crescent Creamery, Rochester, Minn., called at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: A shooting affair took place in Little Mo., today in which Ed. Severson was shot through the thum and fore finger and side, the bullet entering the right side between the hip and last rib, not necessarily fatal. The person doing the shooting was foreman for Webo, and has left the town. He was known Perfect.
articles.summary: Ed. Severson shot and wounded in Little Missouri by a foreman for Webo, who left town.

articles.text: T. H. Van Voorhis of Beallsville Pa. arrived last Friday with a car load of bulls for the LeMoyne Cattle Co. There was one full blood Devon and eighteen grade Shorthorns. Mr. VanVoorhis expressed himself as well pleased with the country and talks of putting in some cattle or horses next spring. He is a promient cattle dealer in the east.
articles.summary: T. H. Van Voorhis delivered a carload of bulls for the LeMoyne Cattle Co.

articles.text: Wm. Higgins a young man who is well known in this country and who lived about six miles from Dickinson, committed suicide at his ranch last Tuesday morning at seven o'clock. He complained of feeling blue, went and set down beside the house, placed a pistol to his head and blowed his brains out. Love was supposed to be the cause of the act.
articles.summary: Wm. Higgins killed himself at his ranch near Dickinson Tuesday morning.

articles.text: The sagacity and affection of animals, especially the horse and dog, for young children and the weak in general, is well known, but has never been so thoroughly exemplified as it was last Sunday morning. Some cruel, blood thirsty cow boys inveigled a little, weak, emaciated boy, just fresh from the green pastures of Chicago, into attempting to ride a broncho, noted for its bucking proclivities. A large and sympathizing crowd collected, fully expecting to see the buttes around covered with the gore of the poor little boy, but the instinct, heretofore mentioned, was possessed by this broncho to a remarkable degree. The crowd cheered and patted "Fatty" on the back, (some of the blows falling a little short and hitting the broncho) but the broncho remained firm and carried Ed. as carefully as if he was a last years egg, and all went well, until the broncho made a misstep in a mud hole and Ed. glided gently into a soft place in the mud. Ed. says he did not have to pay for the drinks and that was the most he cared for. We will only give the initials of the small boy, which are Ed. Meyers as we do not wish to alarm his friends to whom marked copies have been sent.
articles.summary: Mock-heroic account of 'Fatty' Ed. Meyers, newly from Chicago, riding a bucking broncho Sunday morning and landing in the mud.

articles.text: At the examination into the case of Win. Roberts, charged with stealing six horses from the Hash Knife outfit, the testimony of the prosecution was nearly all in when Mr. Middleton, attorney for the defendant, addressed his honor, Judge Staehle, stating that the defense was willing to waive examination. The Judge accordingly fixed the amount of Robert's bail at $2,500 to appear before the district court, and recognized the witnesses to appear also, fixing the bond in the case of one witness for the prosecution at $1,000. Judge Strevell and A. H. O'Conner appeared for the prosecution. The horses in question are part of a lot of nine horses that were stolen from Hughes & Simpson in the spring of '84 and were run north to the Moosomin. The horses were traced to the Moosomin and the principal testimony against the prisoner details his operations there. The story of his arrest has already been told in these columns. It was a notable search and capture by Stock Detective W. D. Smith, who got his man at Rapid City, Dak. Win. Roberts is an old timer in eastern Montana and is well known by many who were here in the early days of freghting and steamboating.—[Yellowstone Journal.
articles.summary: Wm. Roberts, charged with stealing six Hash Knife horses, waived examination and was bound over on $2,500 bail (Yellowstone Journal).
